extracted.intended_audience: writers and critics of fiction and poetry (especially women writers/readers) and literary-minded readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical standards for producing truer, broader fiction and sincere poetry, with emphasis on new subjects opened by women's experience and on authentic, democratic poetic expression. Includes cautions about clichés (forced 'heart interest', passive fairy-tale ideals) and notes on characterization and social realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for broader, truer fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The widening demand for broader, truer fiction is opposed by conservative tastes and by marketers; literature has long been dominated by narrow masculine canons of heroes and repetitive 'one-act play' plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should move beyond the narrow male-dominated staples (repeated heroic one-act plays and enforced 'heart interest') toward broader, truer representations of life. Anti-patterns include publishers insisting that a work must have an injected 'heart interest' (example: David Harum being forced to have one), and the continual recycling of conventional heroes. Examples for contrast: Robert Ellesmere's popularity was not due to manufactured 'heart interest'; Uncle Tom's Cabin succeeded because of its wide human interests rather than a single romantic 'heart interest.'

rubrics_metrics.name: New fields opened by the humanizing of woman (five areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The humanizing of woman opens five distinctly fresh fields of fiction: (1) the young woman asked to give up her 'career' for marriage and who objects; (2) the middle-aged woman who discovers her discontent is social starvation and needs business in life, not more love; (3) the interrelation of women with women (previously little represented outside harems and convents); (4) the long, realistic drama of mother–child relationship beyond the eternal baby trope; (5) the full-grown woman who faces love with the high standards of conscious motherhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should explore these newly available subjects seriously and sympathetically; each is rich ground for novels and will attract broad readership (e.g., 'a million mothers and many million children would eagerly read' realistic mother–child dramas). The list is given as concrete topic-areas to expand fiction beyond traditional male interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overestimating male-dominant instincts (critique of Love-and-War emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our one-sided culture has disproportionately overestimated the dominant instincts of the male—Love and War—an offense against art and truth, and an injury to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fiction should correct this imbalance by depicting a wider range of human motives and experiences, especially those not centered on male-coded drives of romance and conflict. Treating Love and War as the sole dominant instincts is both artistically limiting and socially misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on fairy tales as primary sources for modern ideals of love
rubrics_metrics.description: Using fairy tales and old romance (Grimm's Märchen, Cinderella, Beauty and the Beast, Sleeping Beauty, Elaine) as the highest sources for girls' ideals of love is inadequate and misleading for real-life marriage problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairy tales present passive, romanticized models (e.g., Sleeping Beauty's unconscious surrender; Elaine's absolute ignorance and melodramatic self-destruction) that are inappropriate as guides for adult marriage. Writers and educators should form ideals of love from widest knowledge, highest principles, and practical considerations rather than from these tales. Anti-patterns: presenting marriage as instant surrender, lack of discretion, or theatrical self-sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage and love ideals require wide knowledge, purpose, principle, and practical action
rubrics_metrics.description: Right marriage is a matter calling for the widest knowledge, the noblest purpose, the highest principles, the most practical action; it concerns private happiness and broad social duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating love and marriage in fiction (or advising on ideals), present them as responsible undertakings with consequences—formed by mature reflection and social awareness—not as rosy dreams for 'girls and boys.' Emphasize adult responsibility and social implications rather than romanticized innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should be sincere, genuine, and democratically inclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is a natural form of expression for most human beings; there is as much room for short-distance (local, modest) poetry as for the great world-ringing poet. Valuable poetry is 'clear sincerity' in feeling and expression; verses should not be 'cooked' but should 'grow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage democratic participation in poetry—shorter, sincere pieces have their place alongside canonical works. Evaluate poems on genuine contribution, authentic voice, and honest feeling ('real speech of an honest soul'). Anti-patterns: overworked or contrived verse, exclusivist gatekeeping that reserves poetic value only for few 'great' poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: depict decisiveness and respect women's professional agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who 'wabble' through life without decision are weakly drawn; portrayals that assume a woman's immediate surrender of career for a man's convenience (e.g., 'You are a woman, and I am a man—and I love you') are a harmful cliché.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters with agency and believable motives; avoid protagonists whose primary trait is indecision. Do not normalise male presumptions that women will abandon work or vocation on demand—such assumptions are poor character motivation and diminish realism. Use incidents (e.g., the heroine who gives up her illustrating work because a suitor assumes it) as cautionary examples of bad plotting and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent realistic domestic and social arrangements for working women
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern unmarried women may live together, form residence clubs, or manage boarding-houses; these alternatives provide real 'homes' and satisfying social life outside traditional family structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction should depict the practical realities and satisfactions of alternative living arrangements (boarding-houses, clubs), labor conditions (wages, costs, household economics), and the social independence of women. Examples in the text (the successful boarding-house run by Mrs. Joyce) illustrate how to render such scenes with detail (budgets, staffing, furnishings) and dignity rather than sentimentality.
